content:
1. Introduction

The Indian Constitution did not appear suddenly in 1950. It is the result of nearly 175 years of constitutional development, starting from the Regulating Act of 1773 and ending with the work of the Constituent Assembly (1946-1949). Many features we see today, such as the federal structure, the Governor, the Public Service Commissions, the Federal Court and the three-list division of powers, were first introduced by the British laws passed during this period.

For exams, this chapter is important because questions are asked on: which Act introduced what, who was the first person in a post, and the facts of the Constituent Assembly. This chapter explains all of them in simple steps.

The whole story can be divided into three phases:

Company Rule (1773-1858): The East India Company rules, and the British Parliament slowly takes control.

Crown Rule (1858-1947): The British Crown rules directly, and Indians gradually get a share in government.

Constitution Making (1946-1950): Indians write their own Constitution.

2. Phase 1: Company Rule (1773-1858)

2.1 Regulating Act, 1773

This was the first step taken by the British Parliament to control and regulate the East India Company's affairs in India. Before this, the Company worked almost like a private trading body with very little supervision.

Key provisions:

The Governor of Bengal was made the Governor-General of Bengal. Warren Hastings was the first.

An Executive Council of four members was created to assist the Governor-General.

The Governors of Bombay and Madras were placed under the Governor-General of Bengal.

A Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta in 1774 (one Chief Justice and three judges). Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice.

Company servants were banned from private trade and from taking gifts or bribes from Indians.

The Company's Court of Directors had to report its revenue, civil and military affairs to the British government.

Why it matters: It was the first time British Parliament formally intervened in the Company's rule. It is the starting point of constitutional history in almost every exam.

2.2 Amending Act (Act of Settlement), 1781

This Act fixed problems created by the 1773 Act. It clarified the relationship between the Governor-General and the Supreme Court. The Governor-General and Council were exempted from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction for acts done in their official capacity. The Act also recognised that Hindu and Muslim personal laws would be applied to Hindus and Muslims.

2.3 Pitt's India Act, 1784

Named after the British Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger.

Key provisions:

It separated the Company's commercial functions from its political functions.

The Court of Directors looked after commercial matters.

A new body, the Board of Control, was created to manage political affairs. This is called the dual system of control.

The Governor-General's Council was reduced from four members to three.

It gave the British government clear and final authority over the Company's Indian territories.

2.4 Charter Act, 1793

It extended the Company's trade monopoly for another 20 years. It also made the salaries of the Board of Control members payable from Indian revenue.

2.5 Charter Act, 1813

It ended the Company's trade monopoly in India, except for the trade in tea and with China.

It allotted Rs. 1 lakh every year for education of Indians. This was the first time the British state accepted some responsibility for education.

It allowed Christian missionaries to work in India.

It clearly stated the Crown's sovereignty over Company territories.

2.6 Charter Act, 1833 (Very Important)

This is one of the most important Acts of the Company period.

The Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India. Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India.

The Company's trade monopoly ended fully. It became only an administrative body.

All legislative powers were centralised in the Governor-General-in-Council. Bombay and Madras lost their law-making powers.

A fourth member, the Law Member, was added to the Governor-General's Council. Lord Macaulay was the first Law Member.

It stated that no Indian would be denied a government job only because of religion, birth, descent or colour. (This was not properly followed in practice.)

2.7 Charter Act, 1853

The last of the Charter Acts.

It separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council. A separate Legislative Council with 6 additional legislative members was created. This was like a mini-Parliament and followed the model of the British Parliament.

It introduced open competition for civil service selection. Indians could now also appear. (Macaulay Committee, 1854.)

The Law Member became a full member of the Executive Council.

It did not fix a time limit for the Company's rule, so the Company's rule could be ended at any time.

3. Phase 2: Crown Rule (1858-1947)

After the Revolt of 1857, the British government decided that the Company could no longer be trusted to run India.

3.1 Government of India Act, 1858

It ended the rule of the East India Company. India came directly under the British Crown.

The Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished.

A new post of Secretary of State for India was created, a British Cabinet minister who ran Indian affairs. He was helped by a 15-member Council of India.

The Governor-General of India got the new title Viceroy. Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of India.

Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858) promised religious tolerance and equal treatment.

3.2 Indian Councils Act, 1861

It started the portfolio system (the Viceroy's Council members were given separate departments).

It allowed the Viceroy to nominate non-official Indians to the Legislative Council. In 1862 Lord Canning nominated three Indians: the Raja of Benares, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.

It restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras (taken away in 1833). This began the process of decentralisation.

It gave the Viceroy the power to issue ordinances in an emergency (valid for 6 months).

3.3 Indian Councils Act, 1892

It increased the number of non-official (additional) members in the Central and Provincial Legislative Councils.

It gave councils the power to discuss the budget and to ask questions (but not supplementary questions).

It introduced the principle of indirect election in a limited way (members were still officially "nominated" on the recommendation of bodies such as municipalities and universities).

3.4 Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms)

Named after Lord Morley (Secretary of State) and Lord Minto (Viceroy).

The size of the Central Legislative Council was increased from 16 to 60 members.

It introduced separate electorates for Muslims. Because of this, Lord Minto is called the "Father of Communal Electorate".

It introduced the principle of direct election for the first time (in a limited way).

It allowed members to ask supplementary questions and move resolutions on the budget.

It appointed the first Indian member to the Viceroy's Executive Council: Satyendra Prasad Sinha (law member).

3.5 Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)

Named after Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy). It followed the August 1917 declaration that the British aim was the gradual introduction of "responsible government".

Key provisions:

Dyarchy (dual government) in the provinces. Provincial subjects were divided into:

Transferred subjects (education, health, local government, agriculture), managed by Indian ministers answerable to the legislature.

Reserved subjects (law and order, finance, land revenue, justice), managed by the Governor and his executive council.

A bicameral legislature at the Centre: the Council of State (upper house) and the Central Legislative Assembly (lower house). Majority of members were directly elected.

Separate electorates were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.

It separated the central and provincial budgets (from 1921).

It provided for a High Commissioner for India in London.

It provided for the creation of a Public Service Commission (established in 1926).

A statutory commission was to be appointed after 10 years (this led to the Simon Commission).

3.7 Government of India Act, 1935 (Most Important Act)

This is the longest and most important pre-Independence Act. It had 321 sections and 10 schedules. A large part of today's Constitution (about 250 provisions) was borrowed from it. This is why it is called the "blueprint of the Indian Constitution".

Key provisions:

Proposed an All-India Federation of British provinces and princely states. This never came into force because the princes did not agree.

Abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced Provincial Autonomy. Provinces were now free to govern in their own sphere.

Introduced dyarchy at the Centre (Federal and Reserved subjects). This part was never implemented.

Divided powers into three lists: Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54 items) and Concurrent List (36 items). Residuary powers were given to the Governor-General.

Established a Federal Court (1937) in Delhi. It was the predecessor of the Supreme Court.

Established the Reserve Bank of India (1935).

Provided for a Federal Public Service Commission, Provincial Public Service Commissions and Joint Public Service Commissions.

Created bicameral legislatures in 6 provinces (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces).

Extended separate electorates to the depressed classes, women and labour.

Increased the number of voters: about 10 percent of the population got the right to vote.

Separated Burma from India (1937) and created the new provinces of Sind and Orissa.

Abolished the Council of India and the post of Secretary of State's advisers.

Provincial elections of 1937: The Congress won in 8 out of 11 provinces and formed governments.

3.9 Indian Independence Act, 1947

It ended British rule on 15 August 1947 and created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan.

The Crown's sovereignty over the princely states ended.

The post of Viceroy ended; each dominion got a Governor-General. Lord Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of independent India.

The Constituent Assembly of each dominion was given the power to make its own constitution and was also made the legislature of the dominion until a new constitution came in.

The Secretary of State for India's post was ended.

4. Phase 3: Making of the Constitution (1946-1950)

4.1 Demand for a Constituent Assembly

1934: M.N. Roy first proposed the idea of a Constituent Assembly for India.

1935: The Indian National Congress officially demanded it.

1938: Jawaharlal Nehru declared that the Constitution should be framed without outside interference by a Constituent Assembly elected on adult franchise.

1940: The British accepted the demand in principle through the August Offer.

1946: The Cabinet Mission Plan gave the final scheme.

4.2 Composition of the Constituent Assembly

Total proposed strength: 389 members (296 from British India and 93 from the princely states).

Members were indirectly elected by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies. They were not elected on adult franchise.

In the elections of July-August 1946, the Congress won 208 seats out of 296 and the Muslim League won 73.

After the partition, the strength fell to 299 (284 members were present on 24 January 1950 to sign the Constitution).

15 women were members (for example Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Sucheta Kripalani, Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit).

The Assembly was not a body of the Congress alone: it included representatives of many views, such as B.R. Ambedkar and Frank Anthony.

Today, after many amendments, it has about 448 Articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.

6. Common Exam Traps

Governor-General of Bengal (1773) vs Governor-General of India (1833): Do not mix Warren Hastings with William Bentinck.

Governor-General vs Viceroy: The title Viceroy began in 1858 (Lord Canning), after Company rule ended.

Dyarchy in the provinces (1919) vs the Centre (1935): The 1919 Act introduced it in the provinces, and it worked. The 1935 Act proposed it for the Centre, but it was never implemented.

Cabinet Mission (1946) vs Cripps Mission (1942): Cripps came during the war and failed. The Cabinet Mission gave the structure of the Constituent Assembly.

Father of the Constitution vs Constitutional Adviser: Ambedkar is chairman of the Drafting Committee; B.N. Rau was the Constitutional Adviser.

Date of adoption vs date of enforcement: 26 November 1949 (adopted) and 26 January 1950 (came into force). 26 November is celebrated as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).

7. Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten Plan and the Last Steps in Detail

7.1 Cabinet Mission Plan (March-May 1946)

The Cabinet Mission had three British ministers: Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State), Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander. It rejected the Muslim League's demand for a separate Pakistan, but it did not want a very strong Centre either. It gave a middle path.

A three-tier structure: the Union at the top, Groups of provinces in the middle, and provinces at the bottom.

The Union would control only foreign affairs, defence and communications, with the power to raise the money needed for them. All other subjects were with the provinces.

Provinces were placed in three Groups: Group A (mainly Hindu-majority provinces such as Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, Central Provinces and Orissa), Group B (Punjab, Sind, North-West Frontier Province and Baluchistan) and Group C (Bengal and Assam).

A Constituent Assembly of 389 members was to be formed. Seats were divided among provinces by population (roughly one member for every 10 lakh people) and shared among the Muslim, Sikh and General communities.

An Interim Government of Indian leaders was to run the country till the Constitution was ready.

The Congress and the Muslim League both accepted the plan at first. The Muslim League later withdrew its acceptance and announced Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946.

The Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946 with Jawaharlal Nehru as its head (Vice-President of the Executive Council).

7.2 Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)

As communal violence grew, the new Viceroy Lord Mountbatten announced that India would be divided into two countries.

Muslim-majority areas could form Pakistan. Bengal and Punjab were to be divided by a Boundary Commission headed by Cyril Radcliffe.

The princely states were free to join India or Pakistan. (Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon integrated most of them with India.)

The date of transfer of power was advanced to 15 August 1947.

The Constituent Assembly of India continued its work, with its members reduced to 299 after the areas that became Pakistan left.

7.3 After Independence

From 15 August 1947, the Constituent Assembly worked as both a constitution-making body and the Dominion Legislature (Parliament). When it met as the legislature, G.V. Mavalankar presided, and he later became the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

Until the new Constitution came, India was governed under the Government of India Act, 1935, with necessary changes.

Article 395 of the Constitution repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935.

According to standard textbooks, about 7,600 amendments were proposed and about 2,400 of them were actually moved and discussed (approximate figures).

8. Objectives Resolution and How the Present Constitution Is Linked to the Earlier Laws

8.1 Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946)

This was the philosophical base of the Constitution. Its main points were:

India is an Independent Sovereign Republic.

India will be a Union of British Indian territories, Indian states and other territories willing to join.

All power and authority of the sovereign independent India comes from the people.

Guarantee of justice, equality of status and opportunity, and freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, vocation, association and action.

Adequate safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed and other backward classes.

The territorial integrity of the Republic will be maintained.

India will make its full and willing contribution to world peace and the welfare of mankind.

The Preamble of the Constitution is based on this Resolution.

8.3 Why These Early Laws Still Matter

The British laws were not made to give Indians freedom. Each one was passed to meet a British need: to control the Company, to calm Indian anger after 1857, or to share a little power. But they gave India many things the framers later used: a trained civil service, a central legislature, a court system, the habit of debate in legislatures, and a federal division of powers. The framers kept what worked and added what Indians had demanded for decades: universal adult franchise, fundamental rights, an independent judiciary, and a secular, democratic republic.

9. Key Points to Remember (Last-Minute Revision)

1773 = Regulating Act = first parliamentary control = Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774).

1784 = Pitt's India Act = Board of Control = dual system.

1833 = Governor-General of India = Bentinck = Macaulay as Law Member.

1853 = last Charter Act = separate Legislative Council = open competition.

1858 = Crown rule = Viceroy (Canning) = Secretary of State.

1861 = portfolio system; 1892 = budget discussion; 1909 = separate electorates.

1919 = dyarchy in provinces = bicameral Centre.

1935 = provincial autonomy = Federal Court = RBI = blueprint of the Constitution.

1947 = Independence Act = India and Pakistan.

Constituent Assembly: first meeting 9 Dec 1946; Drafting Committee 29 Aug 1947; adopted 26 Nov 1949; effective 26 Jan 1950.

content:
1. Introduction

Chapter 1 told the story of how constitutional development moved from the Regulating Act of 1773 to the Cabinet Mission of 1946. This chapter explains how the Constituent Assembly actually worked: who sat in it, which committees did what, how decisions were taken, what criticism it faced and from where the Constitution borrowed its ideas.

A Constituent Assembly is a body elected or formed specially to write a country's constitution. The idea came from the American Revolution and the French Revolution. In India, the demand grew in the 1930s because Indians wanted the Constitution to be written by Indians themselves, not given by the British Parliament.

This chapter is important for exams because most questions on this topic ask for names of committees and their chairmen, numbers (members, days, Articles), and the foreign sources of the Constitution.

2. Why a Constituent Assembly Was Needed

Self-rule: Earlier constitutions of India (1858, 1861, 1892, 1909, 1919, 1935) were all passed by the British Parliament. Indians wanted a constitution made by their own representatives.

Sovereignty of the people: The idea that the final power belongs to the people can only be realised if the people's representatives write the rules.

Unity of a diverse country: India had many religions, languages, provinces and princely states. A common, agreed document was needed to hold them together.

Legitimacy: A Constitution written after open debate by many groups is accepted more easily than one imposed from outside.

Steps in the demand (revision from Chapter 1)

1935

1946

Cabinet Mission gave the plan and elections were held

3. Composition of the Constituent Assembly

3.1 Number of Members

Planned strength: 389 = 296 from British Indian provinces + 93 from princely states.

Of the 296 British Indian seats, 292 were from the Governors' provinces (11 provinces) and 4 from the Chief Commissioners' provinces (Delhi, Ajmer-Merwara, Coorg and British Baluchistan).

After partition (3 June 1947), members from areas that became Pakistan left. The Assembly's strength fell to 299.

On 24 January 1950, 284 members were present and signed the Constitution.

3.2 How Members Were Chosen

Members from British India were indirectly elected by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies. The voters were therefore limited in number, as only a small part of the population had the right to vote then.

Members from princely states were nominated by the heads of those states.

Seats were divided on the basis of population: roughly one seat for every 10 lakh people.

In each province, seats were divided among three communities: Muslims, Sikhs and General (all others), in proportion to their population. Each community's members were elected by its own members in the provincial assembly.

3.3 Result of the 1946 Elections

The Muslim League first took part in the elections, but then boycotted the Assembly's meetings demanding a separate Pakistan, so it did not attend the first session.

3.4 Who Were the Members?

The Assembly was dominated by the Congress, but it also included leaders from many views and communities, and many experts.

Congress leaders: Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, Govind Ballabh Pant.

Legal experts: B.R. Ambedkar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B.N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser, not a member).

Minority and tribal voices: Frank Anthony (Anglo-Indians), H.C. Mukherjee (Christians), Jaipal Singh Munda (tribals).

Other parties and groups: Syama Prasad Mookerjee (Hindu Mahasabha), Dr. Ambedkar (Scheduled Castes Federation).

Women members (15): Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Sucheta Kripalani, Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, Ammu Swaminathan, Dakshayani Velayudhan, Begum Aizaz Rasul and others.

Bihar's role: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (President of the Assembly), Sachchidananda Sinha (first temporary president) and Anugrah Narayan Sinha were among the Bihar members.

Note on Ambedkar: Ambedkar was first elected from Bengal. After partition the seat went to Pakistan, so he was elected from Bombay with Congress support.

4.2 How Decisions Were Taken

Committees first: Most of the detailed work was done in committees. They submitted reports to the Assembly.

Debate: Members discussed each Article of the draft. Anyone could suggest amendments.

Voting: Decisions were taken by majority, but leaders tried to reach consensus, especially on difficult issues such as language, minority rights and the role of the states.

Public participation: Draft proposals were published in newspapers and the public sent suggestions.

Expert help: B.N. Rau prepared the initial draft after studying many world constitutions and talking to leaders abroad.

4.4 Important Facts of Adoption

The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

Some Articles came into force immediately on that day: Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393. These deal with citizenship, the election of the President, the Election Commission, definitions and the interim Parliament.

The rest of the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, which is called the date of commencement.

26 January was chosen to honour Poorna Swaraj Day (1930).

The Government of India decided to observe 26 November as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) from 2015.

7. Sources of the Indian Constitution (Borrowed Features)

The framers studied the constitutions of many countries and took only those features that suited Indian conditions. This is why the Indian Constitution is called a "bag of borrowings", though the framers combined them with Indian needs.

Easy trick: India took the Federation from Canada, the Rights from America, the Rule of Law from Britain, the Directive Principles from Ireland, and the Concurrent List from Australia.

8. Criticism of the Constituent Assembly

The Assembly is remembered with great respect, but its critics have raised some points. Students should know both sides.

Criticism

Reply given by supporters

At that time, holding a nationwide election on adult franchise was not possible; the Assembly included many communities and viewpoints

Not a sovereign body: it was created under the Cabinet Mission Plan, a British proposal

After 15 August 1947 the Assembly became fully sovereign and was no longer bound by the plan

Leaders like Nehru and Prasad accommodated the views of other parties; Ambedkar, an opponent of the Congress, chaired the Drafting Committee

Lawyer-politician domination: many members were lawyers

Legal experts helped in drafting a precise legal document

Time-consuming: it took almost three years

The Constitution is a large and complex document that needed full discussion

Hindu domination: a charge made by some critics

The Assembly had members from all major communities and included strong protection for minorities

9. Why the Constituent Assembly Is Called Great

It produced a long, detailed and flexible Constitution that has worked for more than 75 years.

It balanced different needs: a strong Centre but also states, individual rights but also social justice, a secular state but also respect for religion.

Its debates (published as the Constituent Assembly Debates) are used by the Supreme Court to understand the meaning of the Constitution.

It was an example of consensus, discussion and compromise among people of very different opinions.

10. Quick Revision Points

Constituent Assembly strength: 389 planned, 299 after partition, 284 signed.

Congress won 208, Muslim League 73 of the 296 British Indian seats.

First meeting 9 Dec 1946; Objectives Resolution moved 13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947.

Permanent President: Dr. Rajendra Prasad. Constitutional Adviser: B.N. Rau.

Drafting Committee formed 29 Aug 1947, Chairman Dr. Ambedkar, 7 members.

Draft introduced 4 Nov 1948; adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950.

Time taken: 2 years 11 months 18 days; 165 days of sittings; 114 days on the draft.

At adoption: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules.

Articles in force from 26 Nov 1949: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393.

Chief calligraphers: Prem Behari Narain Raizada (English), Vasant Krishan Vaidya (Hindi).

content:
At a Glance: The Preamble in 6 Lines

The Preamble is the short introduction at the beginning of the Constitution.

It tells us who made the Constitution (the people of India), what kind of country India is and what the Constitution wants to achieve.

India is a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.

The four goals are Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution of Jawaharlal Nehru (1946-47).

It was amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

If you remember only these six lines, you already know the core of this chapter. The rest of the chapter explains each line one by one.

1. What Is a Preamble?

A preamble is an introduction to a document. The Preamble of the Indian Constitution is a short statement placed before Article 1. It does not give any right and does not create any duty. Instead, it explains the spirit and the purpose of the Constitution.

Think of it as the mission statement of a country. When a court or a student is unsure what an Article means, the Preamble shows the aim the framers had in mind.

Where does it come from? The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947 (see Chapter 1 and Chapter 2). The Preamble itself was adopted by the Assembly at the end, on 26 November 1949, after all other Articles were passed.

2. The Full Text of the Preamble (As It Stands Today)

WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:

JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;

IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

The Three Easy Parts of the Preamble

The Preamble can be divided into three simple parts. If you remember this division, the whole text becomes easy.

Part

Words in the Preamble

What it tells us

1. Source of authority

"We, the people of India"

The Constitution gets its power from the people, not from any king or foreign ruler

2. Nature of the State

"Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic"

What type of country India is

3. Objectives

"Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity"

What the Constitution wants to give every citizen

(Closing)

"Adopt, enact and give to ourselves"

The date and the act of making the Constitution: 26 November 1949

3. Source of Authority: "We, the People of India"

These opening words show that the Constitution was made by Indians and for Indians. The final power (sovereignty) belongs to the people.

The people act through their representatives, who sat in the Constituent Assembly.

The phrase "We, the people" is similar to the opening of the American Constitution.

The Preamble also uses three verbs: adopt, enact and give. They show that the people themselves took the decision and nobody imposed the Constitution on them.

4. Nature of the State: Five Key Words Explained

Each of the five words below describes one feature of India. The table gives the meaning in simple words, then the sections after it explain each word in detail.

Word (English)

Word (Hindi)

One-line meaning

Sovereign

संप्रभु

India is free and takes its own decisions, inside and outside the country

Socialist

समाजवादी

The State works to reduce the gap between rich and poor

Secular

पंथनिरपेक्ष

The State has no religion of its own and treats all religions equally

Democratic

लोकतंत्रात्मक

Government is chosen by the people through elections

Republic

गणराज्य

The head of the State is elected, not born into the post

4.1 Sovereign

Meaning: Supreme authority. India is not under the control of any other country.

Internal sovereignty: The government has full power to make laws inside India.

External sovereignty: India decides its own foreign policy and is free from foreign control.

Important: India's membership of the Commonwealth of Nations (as an equal partner) or the United Nations does not reduce its sovereignty.

In practice, the Government can still accept international agreements by its own choice.

4.2 Socialist

This word was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

India follows democratic socialism, not the Soviet-style system in which the State owns everything.

Democratic socialism means a mixed economy: the private sector and the public sector work together, and the State acts to remove poverty, inequality and exploitation.

The Constitution already contained the idea of socialism in the Directive Principles (for example, Articles 38, 39 and 41).

The Supreme Court has said that the aim of socialism is to give a decent standard of living to everyone and to reduce differences in income and status.

4.3 Secular

This word was also added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Even before 1976, India was secular in spirit. Articles 25 to 28 give freedom of religion, and Article 15 prevents discrimination on the ground of religion.

The Indian model of secularism is "equal respect for all religions" (sarva dharma sambhava). It is different from the Western idea, in which religion and the State are kept strictly apart.

Features of Indian secularism:

The State has no official religion.

Every person is free to follow, practise and spread their own religion (subject to public order, morality and health).

The State does not discriminate against any citizen on the basis of religion.

The State can still make laws on social reform in religious practices (for example, abolition of untouchability).

The Supreme Court in the S.R. Bommai case (1994) held that secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

4.4 Democratic

Democracy means that power rests with the people, who choose their government through free and fair elections based on universal adult franchise (every citizen aged 18 and above has the right to vote; Article 326).

India is a representative (indirect) democracy: people elect representatives who make laws and run the government.

The word covers three types of democracy:

Political democracy: one person, one vote.

Social democracy: equality in social life; no discrimination.

Economic democracy: a fair share of resources and opportunities.

In his speech to the Assembly, Dr. Ambedkar warned that political democracy cannot last unless it rests on social democracy.

Tools of direct democracy such as referendum, initiative and recall are not used at the national level in India.

4.5 Republic

A republic is a State in which the head of the State is elected and holds office for a fixed term.

India's head of state is the President, who is indirectly elected for five years (Article 54 and 56).

In a monarchy (for example, the United Kingdom), the head of the State comes to the post by birth and usually holds it for life.

A republic also means that no special privileges are held by any class. All public offices are open to all citizens.

India became a republic on 26 January 1950.

Note: The word republic in India does not mean the head of the Government is elected directly. It only means the head of the State (the President) is not hereditary.

5. Objectives of the Constitution: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity

The Preamble lists four goals which the State wants to secure for all its citizens.

5.1 Justice (न्याय)

Justice has three types:

Type

Meaning

Where it is found in the Constitution

Social justice

No discrimination on the basis of caste, religion, sex or birth

Fundamental Rights (Articles 14-17), reservation provisions

Economic justice

No discrimination on the basis of income, wealth or economic status; fair distribution of wealth

Directive Principles (Articles 39, 41, 43)

Political justice

Equal political rights for all: voting, contesting elections, holding public office

Articles 325-326 (equal voting right), Part V and Part VI

The ideal of justice (social, economic and political) was taken from the Russian Revolution (1917).

5.2 Liberty (स्वतंत्रता)

Preamble lists five liberties: thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.

Liberty does not mean doing anything one likes. It means freedom within the limits of law and the rights of others.

These liberties are protected by the Fundamental Rights: Article 19 (freedom of speech and expression) and Articles 25-28 (freedom of religion).

5.3 Equality (समता)

The Preamble talks of equality of status and equality of opportunity.

Equality of status means that all are equal before the law (Article 14), and that titles and untouchability are abolished (Articles 17 and 18).

Equality of opportunity means all citizens have an equal chance in public employment (Article 16).

Equality does not mean everyone is treated exactly the same. The Constitution allows special provisions (for example, reservation) to help weaker sections reach the same level.

5.4 Fraternity (बंधुता)

Fraternity means a feeling of brotherhood among all Indians.

The Preamble says fraternity must assure two things:

Dignity of the individual: Every person must be treated with respect.

Unity and integrity of the Nation: The country must remain united and undivided. The words "and integrity" were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) also encourage fraternity.

Dr. Ambedkar said that without fraternity, liberty and equality cannot be real.

5.5 Where Did These Ideals Come From?

Ideal in the Preamble

Source of the idea

"We, the people" and the idea of people's sovereignty

American Constitution

Liberty, Equality and Fraternity

French Revolution (1789)

Justice: social, economic and political

Russian Revolution (1917)

Republic

French model

Objectives and general aims

Objectives Resolution (Nehru, 1946-47)

Dr. Ambedkar said that he took the ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity not only from the French Revolution but also from the teaching of the Buddha.

6. The Date in the Preamble

The Preamble says the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. But only some Articles came into force on that day. The whole Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. That is why Republic Day is on 26 January, while Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) is observed on 26 November.

7. Amendment of the Preamble

The Preamble has been amended only once so far, by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. This Act was passed during the Emergency and is called the "Mini-Constitution" because it changed many parts of the Constitution. It followed the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

Before 1976

After 1976

Sovereign Democratic Republic

Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic

Unity of the Nation

Unity and Integrity of the Nation

Words added in 1976 (remember three): Socialist, Secular, Integrity.

The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) allowed the Preamble to be amended as long as the basic structure is not changed. The 1976 amendment was made on this basis. The date "26 November 1949" in the Preamble was not changed, because the Constituent Assembly had adopted the Preamble on that date.

8. Is the Preamble a Part of the Constitution?

This is the part of the chapter that causes the most confusion. The simple answer is:

Today, the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution. The Supreme Court first said No (1960) and then changed its view to Yes (1973). The later decision is the law.

The table below shows the full journey in the correct order.

Year

Case

What the Supreme Court decided

1960

Berubari Union case (In re Berubari Union, an opinion given to the President under Article 143)

The Preamble is the key to open the minds of the framers and helps in understanding the Constitution, but it is not a part of the Constitution

1973

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

The Court overruled the Berubari view. The Preamble is a part of the Constitution. It can be amended under Article 368, but the basic structure cannot be changed

1995

LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre

The Court again said that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution

Easy memory line: Berubari said No (1960), Kesavananda said Yes (1973), LIC said Yes again (1995).

9. Legal Value of the Preamble

Even though it is a part of the Constitution, the Preamble has some limits. Students often mix these up, so read the points one by one.

It is not enforceable in a court of law. A person cannot go to court and demand a remedy only on the basis of the Preamble. A right must be found in an Article (for example, Article 21).

It is not the source of power of Parliament. Parliament gets its powers from the Articles, not from the Preamble.

It does not limit the powers of the legislature. Parliament cannot be stopped from making a law merely because it appears to go against the Preamble. The law must break a specific Article.

It helps in interpretation. When the wording of an Article is unclear, courts use the Preamble to understand the intention of the framers.

It shows the basic structure. Parts of the Preamble (like democracy, secularism, republican form of government, sovereignty) are treated as part of the basic structure.

In simple words: the Preamble guides, but it does not command.

10. What Great Thinkers Said About the Preamble

Person

Description of the Preamble

K.M. Munshi

"Political horoscope" of the Constitution

Thakur Das Bhargava

"Soul" of the Constitution

Ernest Barker

"Key-note" of the Constitution

N.A. Palkhivala

"Identity card" of the Constitution

These descriptions are often asked in exams. Remember K.M. Munshi (horoscope), Thakur Das Bhargava (soul), Ernest Barker (key-note) and N.A. Palkhivala (identity card).

11. Clearing the Common Confusions

These are the points where students usually make mistakes. Each one is given as a simple statement with the correct fact.

Confusion

Correct fact

Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution?

Yes, since the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). The earlier Berubari view (1960) is no longer followed

Which words were added in 1976?

Socialist, Secular and Integrity

Was the Preamble amended more than once?

No. Only once (1976)

Can we go to court on the basis of the Preamble?

Not directly. It is not enforceable; rights come from the Articles

Did the original Constitution use the word Secular?

No. It was added in 1976, though the spirit was there from the beginning (Articles 25-28)

Is the Preamble the same as the Objectives Resolution?

No. The Preamble is based on the Resolution but is a separate, final text

"Republic" means the head of Government is elected?

No. It means the head of the State (the President) is not hereditary

Does "Socialist" mean the State owns all property?

No. India follows democratic socialism with a mixed economy

Does "Secular" mean the State is against religion?

No. It means the State treats all religions equally

Where is the Preamble placed?

Before Article 1, at the beginning of the Constitution

12. Quick Revision Points

Based on: Objectives Resolution (Nehru, 13 Dec 1946; adopted 22 Jan 1947).

Adopted: 26 November 1949; in force: 26 January 1950.

Nature of the State: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.

Objectives: Justice (social, economic, political); Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); Equality (status and opportunity); Fraternity (dignity of the individual; unity and integrity of the Nation).

Amended once: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 (added Socialist, Secular, Integrity).

Berubari (1960): not part. Kesavananda (1973): part. LIC (1995): part.

Not enforceable in a court of law, and not a source of power or a limit on power.

Sources of ideas: American ("We, the people"), French (Liberty, Equality, Fraternity), Russian (Justice).

Descriptions: Munshi (horoscope), Bhargava (soul), Barker (key-note), Palkhivala (identity card).

13. Related Chapters

Previous: Making of the Constitution and the Constituent Assembly

Next: Salient Features of the Indian Constitution

Also read: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, Amendment of the Constitution

content:
At a Glance: The Constitution in 8 Lines

India has a written Constitution, and it is the longest in the world for a sovereign country.

It is partly rigid and partly flexible, because different parts are amended in different ways.

It is federal in form but has a strong Centre, so it is called "federal with a unitary bias".

It gives us a parliamentary system, where the real power is with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.

It has an independent judiciary and a single court system for the whole country.

It gives citizens Fundamental Rights (can be enforced in court) and guides the government through Directive Principles (cannot be enforced in court).

It lists Fundamental Duties of citizens.

It provides for universal adult franchise, single citizenship, a secular state and emergency powers.

Remember these 8 lines first. Each one is explained in detail below.

1. Introduction

The salient features of a constitution are its most important and special characteristics. These are the points that show what kind of country India is and how it is governed.

Chapters 1 to 3 explained the history, the making and the Preamble. This chapter now answers a simple question: "What are the main features of the Constitution that came out of this process?"

For exams, remember the feature, the Article number (where given) and one example. That is enough for most questions.

Map of the Features

1

2

3

4

5

6

7

Fundamental Rights

8

9

10

11

14

15

16

SC, ST, minorities, backward classes

2. Feature 1: Lengthiest Written Constitution

A written constitution is one that is recorded in a single document. India's Constitution is written. (The British Constitution, by contrast, is mostly unwritten.)

It is the longest written constitution of any sovereign country.

At adoption (1949), it had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Today it has about 448 Articles (the usual textbook count), 25 Parts and 12 Schedules, because many Articles and Schedules were added by amendments.

Why is it so long?

The framers borrowed many provisions from other constitutions (see Chapter 2).

It contains the administrative details of both the Centre and the States, which other constitutions often leave to ordinary laws.

It covers special problems of India: backward classes, tribal areas, minorities, and the large number of languages.

It includes Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties in great detail.

It deals with the whole country in one document, not just the Union as in the USA.

3. Feature 2: Drawn from Many Sources

The framers took ideas from many countries and from the Government of India Act, 1935. They adapted the ideas to Indian needs. This is why the Constitution is sometimes called a "bag of borrowings". The detailed table is given in Chapter 2 (Making of the Constitution).

In short:

From the 1935 Act: federal scheme, Governor, emergency provisions, Public Service Commissions.

From Britain: parliamentary government, rule of law.

From the USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review.

From Ireland: Directive Principles.

From Canada: a strong Centre.

From Australia: the Concurrent List.

4. Feature 3: Blend of Rigidity and Flexibility

A rigid constitution is hard to change. A flexible constitution is easy to change.

India's Constitution is both. Its Article 368 gives three different ways to change it, depending on the subject.

Type of amendment

How it is done

Examples

1. Simple majority (outside Article 368, as an ordinary law)

A majority of members present and voting in each House of Parliament, as with an ordinary law

Admission of new states, change of state boundaries, citizenship, Fifth and Sixth Schedules

2. Special majority (Article 368)

A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting

Most provisions, such as Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

3. Special majority + ratification by states (Article 368)

Special majority in Parliament, plus approval by half of the state legislatures (by simple majority)

Federal provisions: election of the President, powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts, Union-State relations, Seventh Schedule, Article 368 itself

Why this blend? The framers wanted the Constitution to be stable (not changed again and again) but also to grow with time. The Supreme Court added another limit in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure.

(The full details are in the chapter "Amendment of the Constitution".)

5. Feature 4: Federal System with a Unitary Bias

5.1 What Is a Federation?

In a federation, power is divided between a central government and state governments, and both work in their own areas. The USA is a typical federation. In a unitary system, all power is with the central government (for example, the United Kingdom).

The word "federation" does not appear in the Constitution. Article 1 describes India as a "Union of States". Dr. Ambedkar explained the reason: the Indian Union is not the result of an agreement among states, and no state has the right to leave the Union. The states are not "destroyable" by their own will.

5.2 Federal Features of India

Two levels of government: the Centre and the States.

Division of powers in the Seventh Schedule into three lists: the Union List (98 subjects), the State List (59 subjects) and the Concurrent List (52 subjects).

Written Constitution with the Constitution as the supreme law.

Rigid procedure for amending federal provisions (needs state ratification).

Independent Supreme Court to settle disputes between the Centre and states.

Bicameral Parliament: the Rajya Sabha represents the states.

5.3 Unitary (Centralising) Features of India

Strong Centre: the Union List has more important subjects than the State List.

Residuary powers (subjects not in any list) belong to the Centre (Article 248).

Parliament can change state boundaries and names by an ordinary law (Article 3). States have no say except to give their opinion.

Single citizenship for the whole country.

Integrated judiciary with the Supreme Court at the top.

All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFS) shared by the Centre and states, but controlled mainly by the Centre.

Governors are appointed by the President, and work as the Centre's representative in a state (Article 155).

Emergency provisions can turn the federal system into a unitary one (Article 352 and Article 356).

Parliament can legislate on a State List subject in the national interest (Article 249) or if two or more states ask (Article 252).

Integrated audit and election machinery: one CAG and one Election Commission for the whole country.

Unequal representation of states in the Rajya Sabha (based on population, not equal as in the US Senate).

5.4 What Do We Call It?

Description

Who said it

"Federal in form but unitary in spirit" / "quasi-federal"

K.C. Wheare

"Cooperative federalism"

Granville Austin

"Bargaining federalism"

Morris Jones

"Union of States" (explanation)

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

The Supreme Court, in the S.R. Bommai case (1994), held that federalism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Easy way to remember: India is federal in structure, but in times of crisis it works like a unitary state.

6. Feature 5: Parliamentary System of Government

India follows the parliamentary system (also called the Westminster model or the cabinet system), taken from the United Kingdom. It works at both the Centre and the states.

6.1 Main Features

Nominal head and real head: The President is the nominal head of the State; the Prime Minister is the real head of the Government. At the state level, the Governor is the nominal head and the Chief Minister is the real head.

Collective responsibility: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75). If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole ministry must resign.

Majority party rule: The party (or alliance) that has a majority in the Lok Sabha forms the government.

Double membership: Ministers are members of the legislature and also of the executive.

Leadership of the Prime Minister: He or she is the head of the Council of Ministers.

Dissolution of the lower house: The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Prime Minister.

6.2 Difference from the British System

Point

6.3 Presidential vs Parliamentary System

The framers chose the parliamentary system because India was already familiar with it under British rule and because it makes the government answerable to the representatives of the people.

7. Feature 6: Independent and Integrated Judiciary

Integrated (single) judiciary: India has one hierarchy of courts for both Union and state laws: the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in each state (or group of states), and subordinate courts below. This is different from the USA, which has separate federal and state courts.

Independent judiciary: The judges are protected from the influence of the executive and the legislature. The important safeguards are:

Security of tenure: Judges cannot be removed easily. A Supreme Court or High Court judge can be removed only by Parliament through a special procedure (impeachment).

Salaries and allowances are fixed and charged to the Consolidated Fund, so Parliament cannot reduce them to harm judges.

Separation from the executive in public service (Article 50 advises it).

Power of contempt: The courts can punish those who insult them.

Judicial review: The Supreme Court and High Courts can declare a law unconstitutional if it breaks the Constitution.

Synthesis of two ideas: The Constitution combines the British idea of parliamentary sovereignty with the American idea of judicial supremacy. Parliament can amend the Constitution, but the Supreme Court can strike down laws and amendments that destroy the basic structure.

8. Feature 7: Fundamental Rights (Part III)

Part III (Articles 12 to 35) contains the Fundamental Rights. They are called the Magna Carta of India.

They are justiciable: a person whose right is violated can go directly to the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court (Article 226).

They protect citizens against the arbitrary action of the State.

They are not absolute: the State can put reasonable restrictions for public order, morality, health and the security of the State.

Note on the Right to Property: It was a Fundamental Right earlier (Article 31). The 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from Part III. It is now a legal right under Article 300A.

Note on Article 21A: The Right to Education for children aged 6 to 14 years was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).

Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

(The full details are in the chapter "Fundamental Rights".)

9. Feature 8: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)

Part IV (Articles 36 to 51) contains guidelines for the government to follow while making laws and policies.

They are taken from the Irish Constitution.

They are non-justiciable: a court cannot force the government to follow them.

Still, Article 37 says they are "fundamental in the governance of the country".

They aim to create a welfare state and achieve social and economic democracy.

10. Feature 9: Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A)

The original Constitution did not have Fundamental Duties.

They were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, as Article 51A in a new Part IV-A. The idea was inspired by the Constitution of the USSR.

At first there were 10 duties. The 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment (2002): a parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6 to 14 years.

Duties are non-justiciable (courts do not enforce them directly). They remind citizens that rights come with responsibilities.

Some of the duties: respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem; protect the sovereignty and integrity of India; promote harmony; protect the environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property.

11. Feature 10: Secular State

The Constitution does not give any religion the status of an official religion.

Articles 25 to 28 protect freedom of religion. Article 15 prohibits discrimination on the ground of religion.

The Indian model of secularism is "equal respect for all religions".

The word "Secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976). (See Chapter 3.)

12. Feature 11: Universal Adult Franchise

Every citizen aged 18 or above has the right to vote, whatever his or her caste, religion, sex, education or wealth (Article 326).

The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Amendment (1988).

Many countries gave this right to women late. India gave the right to vote to everyone from the beginning, in the first general election of 1951-52.

Elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies are held on this basis.

13. Feature 12: Single Citizenship

In a normal federation like the USA, a person is a citizen of the country and also of his or her state (dual citizenship).

In India, there is only one citizenship: Indian citizenship. A person is not a citizen of a state.

All citizens enjoy the same rights across the country.

Citizenship is governed by Part II (Articles 5 to 11) and the Citizenship Act, 1955.

14. Feature 13: Independent Constitutional Bodies

The Constitution created several independent bodies so that important functions are free from political pressure.

15. Feature 14: Emergency Provisions

The Constitution gives the Centre special powers in a crisis. There are three types of emergency:

Type

Article

When it is declared

Effect

(Emergency provisions were borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935 and the Weimar Constitution of Germany. Details are in the chapter "Emergency Provisions".)

16. Feature 15: Three-Tier Government

Originally, the Constitution provided for two levels: the Centre and the States.

The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Panchayati Raj (Part IX) for villages.

The 74th Amendment (1992) added Municipalities (Part IX-A) for towns and cities.

Both came into force in 1993. This made India a country with three tiers: the Centre, the State and the local government.

17. Feature 16: Special Provisions for Weaker Sections

The Constitution gives special protection to groups that have faced disadvantage.

Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST): Reserved seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; reservation in jobs and education.

Backward classes (OBC): Special provisions for educational and social progress.

Minorities: Right to protect their language, script and culture, and to establish educational institutions (Articles 29 and 30).

Women and children: Special laws can be made for them (Article 15(3)).

Tribal areas: The Fifth and Sixth Schedules provide a special system of administration.

Anglo-Indians: Nomination provision (ended by the 104th Amendment, 2019).

18. Criticism of the Constitution

Students should know that people have also criticised the Constitution. Knowing both sides helps in answer writing.

Criticism

Reply

"Borrowed" constitution (a "carbon copy")

The framers selected features after careful study and adapted them; Ambedkar said that borrowing is not a fault

The country is large and diverse, so details were needed

Gandhian ideas are included in the Directive Principles

Needed to keep the country united after Partition

Not made by a directly elected body

Explained in Chapter 2

19. Clearing the Common Confusions

Confusion

Correct fact

Both in part. Federal in structure, but with a strong unitary bias. It is called quasi-federal

No. Article 1 says "Union of States"

No. Reasonable restrictions can be imposed

No. They are non-justiciable

Not directly. They are non-justiciable

42nd Amendment, 1976

20. Quick Revision Points

Written, lengthy Constitution: 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules at the start; about 448 Articles, 25 Parts and 12 Schedules now.

Rigid and flexible: three ways of amendment (simple majority; special majority; special majority plus half of the states).

Federal with unitary bias: Article 1 "Union of States"; Union 98, State 59, Concurrent 52; residuary powers with the Centre (Article 248).

Parliamentary system: Articles 74 and 75; collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.

Integrated and independent judiciary, judicial review.

Fundamental Rights: Part III, Articles 12-35; six rights; Article 32 is the remedy.

DPSP: Part IV, Articles 36-51; non-justiciable; from Ireland.

Fundamental Duties: Part IV-A, Article 51A; 42nd Amendment (1976); 11th duty by 86th Amendment (2002).

Universal adult franchise: Article 326; age 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988).

Single citizenship: Part II.

Emergency: Article 352 (national), 356 (state), 360 (financial).

Three tiers: 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), in force 1993.

1. Introduction

What Is a Schedule?

A Schedule is a list or table placed at the end of the Constitution. It contains detailed information that would make the main text too heavy if it were written inside the Articles. The Articles tell us the rule, and the Schedule gives the details (for example, which states exist, or which languages are recognised).

Article, Part and Schedule: What Is the Difference?

Students often mix these three words. The table makes it clear.

Term

Meaning

Example

Article 21: Protection of life and liberty

Part

A group of related Articles under one heading

Part III: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35)

Schedule

A list or table with details, placed at the end

Seventh Schedule: the three Lists of subjects

How Many Schedules?

The Constitution at the time of adoption (1949) had 8 Schedules.

Today it has 12 Schedules. Four were added later by amendments.

2. First Schedule: States and Union Territories

It lists the names of the States and Union Territories and describes their territories.

It is linked to Article 1 (India is a Union of States) and Article 4 (laws made under Articles 2 and 3 for new states are not considered constitutional amendments).

Whenever a new state is created or the name of a state is changed, this Schedule is amended by an ordinary law of Parliament (Article 3).

Today, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories. (Telangana became the 29th state in 2014. In 2019 Jammu and Kashmir was divided into two Union Territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, which reduced the number of states to 28 and raised the Union Territories to 8.)

At the time of adoption, the First Schedule had four categories of states (Part A, B, C and D). After the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (and the 7th Amendment), these were replaced by 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

3. Second Schedule: Salaries and Allowances

This Schedule lists the emoluments (salary), allowances and privileges of high constitutional office holders.

President of India

Governors of States

Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha

Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the State Legislative Assemblies

Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the State Legislative Councils

Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts

Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India

Note: The salary of the Vice-President is not in this Schedule, because he or she is paid as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The amounts are decided by Parliament through laws, and the Schedule only mentions the heads.

4. Third Schedule: Forms of Oaths and Affirmations

This Schedule gives the text (form) of the oath or affirmation taken by various officials when they take office.

Oaths in the Third Schedule are taken by:

Union Ministers

Candidates for election to Parliament

Members of Parliament

Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts

The Comptroller and Auditor General

Candidates for election to the State Legislature

Members of the State Legislature

Important trap: The oaths of the President and the Governor are not in the Third Schedule. They are written inside the Articles themselves: Article 60 (President) and Article 159 (Governor). The Vice-President's oath is in Article 69.

5. Fourth Schedule: Seats in the Rajya Sabha

It decides how many Rajya Sabha seats each State and Union Territory gets, based on population.

The Constitution allows a maximum of 250 members in the Rajya Sabha:

238 representatives of States and Union Territories (elected), and

12 members nominated by the President (people with special knowledge in literature, science, art and social service).

At present, the Rajya Sabha has 245 members: 233 elected representatives of States and UTs (Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have seats) and 12 nominated members.

(Seat numbers can change after a state is reorganised, so always check the latest figure when answering.)

6. Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes

Related to Article 244(1).

It provides for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all states except the four North-Eastern states covered by the Sixth Schedule (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram).

The President has the power to declare an area a Scheduled Area.

Main provisions:

The Governor of the state gives a yearly report to the President on the administration of the Scheduled Areas.

The Governor can stop or change the application of a central or state law in a Scheduled Area.

A Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) is formed in each state with Scheduled Areas. It advises on the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. It has up to 20 members, of whom three-fourths are the Scheduled Tribe representatives in the State Legislative Assembly.

The Governor can make regulations to prohibit or limit transfer of tribal land and to regulate money-lending.

States with Scheduled Areas (10): Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan.

7. Sixth Schedule: Tribal Areas of the North-East

Related to Articles 244(2) and 275(1).

It applies to the tribal areas of four North-Eastern states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

It provides self-rule to tribal people through Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils.

Main provisions:

The tribal areas are autonomous districts within the state.

Each Autonomous District Council normally has up to 30 members: four nominated by the Governor and the rest elected on adult franchise. The term is five years. (The Bodoland Territorial Council is a special case and has a bigger council.)

The Councils can make laws on land, forests (other than reserved forests), shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance, marriage and social customs. These laws need the Governor's assent.

They can set up courts to try cases among tribal people and can collect certain taxes (for example, on land and markets).

8. Seventh Schedule: The Three Lists

Related to Article 246. This Schedule divides the powers of law-making between the Union (Centre) and the States. It has three lists.

List

Who makes the law?

Number of subjects (present)

Examples

Union List

Only Parliament

98

Defence, foreign affairs, railways, banking, currency, atomic energy, citizenship

State List

Only State Legislature (in normal times)

Concurrent List

Education, forests, criminal law, marriage and divorce, trade unions, population control and family planning

Key points:

Residuary powers (subjects not in any list) belong to the Centre (Article 248). This is different from the USA, where residuary powers are with the states.

If there is a conflict between a central law and a state law on a Concurrent List subject, the central law prevails (Article 254).

The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice.

The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and inserted Article 246A, giving both Parliament and State Legislatures the power to make laws on GST.

In the original Constitution the numbers were 97, 66 and 47. The numbers have changed because of amendments.

The idea of three lists was taken from the Government of India Act, 1935, and the Concurrent List from Australia.

9. Eighth Schedule: Languages

It lists the languages recognised by the Constitution.

At the time of adoption there were 14 languages. Today there are 22.

These languages are used for: representation on the Official Language Commission (Article 344), and the Constitution says Hindi should be developed by taking words from them (Article 351).

Being in the Eighth Schedule does not make a language an official language of the Union. Under Article 343, the official language of the Union is Hindi in the Devanagari script.

The 22 Languages

Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu.

Note: The status of a classical language is a separate government decision. It is not the same as being listed in the Eighth Schedule.

10. Ninth Schedule: Land Reform Laws

Added by the First Amendment (1951) along with Article 31B.

At first it contained 13 laws. Later many more laws were added.

Purpose: The government wanted to carry out land reforms (abolition of zamindari). Some courts had struck down these laws because they violated the Right to Property. The Ninth Schedule was created to protect such laws from judicial review.

Today's position (important): In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) can be reviewed by courts if they violate Fundamental Rights that form part of the basic structure.

In simple words: the Ninth Schedule gives protection, but this protection is not absolute.

11. Tenth Schedule: Anti-Defection Law

Added by the 52nd Amendment (1985).

It contains the rules to disqualify a Member of Parliament or a State Legislature who changes party after being elected (called defection).

Related to Articles 102(2) and 191(2).

A member is disqualified if:

He or she voluntarily gives up membership of the party.

He or she votes or abstains against the party's instruction (whip) without permission.

An independent member joins a political party after the election.

A nominated member joins a party after six months of taking a seat.

Exceptions:

If two-thirds of the party's members agree to merge with another party, they are not disqualified.

The Speaker or Chairman can leave the party after being elected to the office and rejoin it after leaving the office.

Who decides? The Presiding Officer (Speaker or Chairman) decides. In the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992), the Supreme Court said that the decision can be reviewed by courts.

91st Amendment (2003): It removed the earlier provision that allowed a one-third split of a party. Now only a two-thirds merger is allowed. It also limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15 percent of the House.

12. Eleventh Schedule: Panchayats

Added by the 73rd Amendment (1992). Related to Article 243G.

It lists 29 subjects on which Panchayats can be given powers.

Examples: agriculture, land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry, fisheries, drinking water, roads, rural housing, poverty alleviation, primary and secondary education, health and sanitation, women and child development, markets and fairs, and libraries.

The State Legislature decides how many of these powers are actually given to Panchayats.

13. Twelfth Schedule: Municipalities

Added by the 74th Amendment (1992). Related to Article 243W.

It lists 18 subjects on which Municipalities (urban local bodies) can be given powers.

Examples: urban planning, regulation of land use and buildings, water supply, public health, sanitation and solid waste management, fire services, urban forestry, slum improvement, burial grounds and public amenities (street lighting, parking, bus stops).

As with Panchayats, the State Legislature decides which powers are given.

12 (8 originally)

16. Quick Revision Points

12 Schedules (8 at the start). Added later: Ninth (1st Amendment 1951), Tenth (52nd 1985), Eleventh and Twelfth (73rd and 74th, 1992).

First: States and UTs (28 States, 8 UTs).

Second: Salaries of President, Governors, Speakers, Judges, CAG.

Third: Oaths (except President, Governor, Vice-President).

Fourth: Rajya Sabha seats (max 250; 238 + 12).

Fifth: Scheduled Areas (10 states). Sixth: Tribal Areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram (10 Autonomous District Councils).

Seventh: Union 98, State 59, Concurrent 52. Residuary powers with the Centre.

Eighth: 22 languages (14 + Sindhi + 3 + 4).

Ninth: Land reforms; reviewable after 24 April 1973 (I.R. Coelho, 2007).

Tenth: Anti-defection (52nd Amendment, 1985); 91st Amendment removed the split rule.

Eleventh: Panchayats, 29 subjects. Twelfth: Municipalities, 18 subjects.
