seo_desc: Easy and complete notes on the amendment of the Indian Constitution: Article 368 procedure, three types of amendment, basic structure doctrine, Kesavananda Bharati case and a list of important amendments (1st to 106th).
content:
At a Glance: Amendment in 8 Lines

Amendment means a formal change in the Constitution (adding, changing or removing a provision).

The procedure is given in Article 368 (Part XX).

Only Parliament can start an amendment (by a Bill in either House). State legislatures cannot.

There are three ways to amend: simple majority, special majority, and special majority plus approval of half of the States.

After the Bill is passed, the President must give assent. He or she cannot send it back.

Parliament cannot change the basic structure of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973).

The Constitution has been amended 106 times (the latest is the 106th Amendment, 2023, on women's reservation).

The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the "Mini-Constitution" because it made the most changes at once.

Learn these 8 lines first. The sections below explain each point.

1. Introduction

No constitution can stay the same forever. Society, the economy and technology change, and the rules must change with them. The framers of the Indian Constitution knew this. They wanted a Constitution that is stable (not changed again and again) and also flexible (able to grow). Chapter 4 explained that India's Constitution is a mix of rigid and flexible. This chapter explains how exactly an amendment is made and what limits exist on it.

Why is amendment needed?

To correct mistakes and fill gaps in the original text.

To respond to new needs (for example GST in 2016 or the local government system in 1992).

To change the balance of power between institutions when needed.

To adopt the changes that come with time, like lowering the voting age to 18.

2. Article 368: The Power and the Procedure

Article 368 (in Part XX) deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure.

2.1 Step-by-Step Procedure

Step

What happens

1. Introduction

A Constitution Amendment Bill is introduced in either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). It can be brought by a minister or a private member. Prior permission of the President is not needed.

2. Passing in each House

The Bill must be passed in each House separately by a special majority (explained below).

3. No joint sitting

If the two Houses disagree, there is no joint sitting. The Bill falls. (A joint sitting is allowed for ordinary Bills but not for amendment Bills.)

4. Ratification by States (only for some subjects)

If the Bill changes a federal provision, it must also be approved by the legislatures of at least half of the States (by simple majority in each).

5. President's assent

The Bill goes to the President. He or she must give assent. He or she cannot withhold it or return it for reconsideration.

6. Law comes into force

After assent, the Constitution stands amended.

Important points:

The Bill cannot be started in a State Legislature. (The only exception: a State Legislature can pass a resolution to create or abolish its Legislative Council, and then Parliament passes a law. This is done under Article 169, and it is not treated as an amendment under Article 368.)

The President's assent became compulsory by the 24th Amendment (1971).

There is no time limit for the States to ratify the Bill.

2.2 What Is a Special Majority?

A special majority means both of the following together:

A majority of the total membership of that House, and

A two-thirds majority of the members present and voting.

Example (Lok Sabha): The Lok Sabha has 543 members.

Majority of total membership: at least 272 members must vote in favour.

If 500 members are present and voting, two-thirds is 334. So the Bill needs at least 334 votes, which is also more than 272.

The special majority is also the rule for some other purposes (for example, removal of a Supreme Court judge).

3. Three Types of Amendment

Type

How it is passed

What it covers

1. Simple majority (an ordinary law, outside Article 368)

A simple majority of members present and voting in each House, as with any ordinary Bill

Admission or creation of new States and change of boundaries (Articles 2, 3, 4); abolition or creation of Legislative Councils (Article 169); citizenship (Article 11); Fifth and Sixth Schedules; salaries and allowances of MPs; quorum; rules of procedure; official language; use of English

2. Special majority (under Article 368)

Special majority in each House

Most provisions: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties and all provisions not covered by types 1 and 3

3. Special majority + ratification by half of the States (under Article 368)

Special majority in Parliament, plus approval by at least half of the State Legislatures

Federal provisions: election of the President (Articles 54, 55); extent of executive power of the Union and States (Articles 73, 162); the Supreme Court and High Courts; distribution of legislative powers between the Union and States; the Seventh Schedule; representation of States in Parliament; and Article 368 itself

Easy way to remember type 3: Anything that affects the powers of the States needs the States to agree.

4. Amendment Procedure of Other Countries (Comparison)

Country

Procedure

USA

Two-thirds of both Houses of Congress (or a convention called by two-thirds of the States), then approval by three-fourths of the States. Very rigid.

UK

Parliament can change constitutional laws by an ordinary law. Very flexible.

India

A mix: simple majority, special majority, or special majority plus half of the States.

The amendment procedure of the Indian Constitution was partly borrowed from the South African Constitution.

5. The Basic Structure Doctrine

This is one of the most important topics of Indian Polity.

5.1 What Is the Basic Structure?

The basic structure doctrine says that Parliament can amend the Constitution, but it cannot destroy or change its basic features. The Constitution does not use the words "basic structure". The idea was created by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).

5.2 The Journey: Cases in the Right Order

Many students get confused because the Supreme Court changed its view several times. The table below shows the full story in time order.

Year

Case

What the Supreme Court said

1951

Shankari Prasad v. Union of India

Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368. An amendment is not "law" under Article 13

1965

Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan

Same view as Shankari Prasad

1967

Golak Nath v. State of Punjab

Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. An amendment is "law" under Article 13

1971

24th Amendment (by Parliament)

Parliament overruled Golak Nath: it can amend any part including Fundamental Rights; amendment is not "law" under Article 13

1973

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot change its basic structure. (Overruled Golak Nath; decided by a 13-judge bench, by a 7:6 majority)

1975

Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain

The Court used the basic structure doctrine to strike down a part of the 39th Amendment (which put the election of the Prime Minister beyond the courts)

1976

42nd Amendment (by Parliament)

Added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368, saying Parliament's amending power has no limits and cannot be questioned in any court

1980

Minerva Mills v. Union of India

The Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368. It said that limited power to amend is itself a basic feature, and that the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure

1981

Waman Rao v. Union of India

The basic structure doctrine applies to amendments made after 24 April 1973

2007

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu

Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review if they damage the basic structure

One-line summary of the journey: Shankari Prasad (Yes) → Sajjan Singh (Yes) → Golak Nath (No) → 24th Amendment (Yes) → Kesavananda (Yes, but not the basic structure).

5.3 Features Treated as Part of the Basic Structure

The Supreme Court has said that the following are part of the basic structure (the list is not fixed; the court adds items in different cases):

Supremacy of the Constitution

Sovereign, democratic and republican nature of the polity

Secular character

Federal character

Parliamentary system of government

Separation of powers

Rule of law

Judicial review

Independence of the judiciary

Free and fair elections

Unity and integrity of the nation

Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

Welfare state

Limited power of Parliament to amend

Powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts under Articles 32 and 226

Important: The basic structure doctrine is a judge-made doctrine, not a written provision of the Constitution.

7. The 42nd Amendment (1976) in Detail: The "Mini-Constitution"

The 42nd Amendment was passed during the Emergency (1975-77), on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. It changed the Constitution so widely that it is called the "Mini-Constitution".

Area

Change

Preamble

Added Socialist, Secular, Integrity

Duties

Added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A)

DPSP

Added new Directive Principles (Articles 39A, 43A, 48A)

Seventh Schedule

Moved 5 subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, administration of justice

Parliament

Lok Sabha term raised to 6 years (later reversed by the 44th)

Judiciary

Limited the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts to review laws

Amendment power

Clauses (4) and (5) added to Article 368; both were struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)

The 44th Amendment (1978) corrected many of these changes after the Emergency.

8. Criticism of the Amendment Procedure

Point

Explanation

No special body

Parliament itself amends the Constitution. There is no separate Constituent Assembly for this purpose

Only Parliament can start it

State legislatures cannot propose an amendment (except the Legislative Council case under Article 169)

Limited role of States

Only a few provisions need State ratification

No time limit

There is no fixed period for States to ratify the Bill

No provision for a deadlock

There is no joint sitting if the two Houses disagree

Too frequent

The Constitution has been amended many times. Supporters reply that most of the amendments were needed to meet changing conditions

9. Clearing the Common Confusions

Confusion

Correct fact

Which Article deals with the amendment?

Article 368 (Part XX)

Can a State Legislature introduce an amendment Bill?

No. Only Parliament can

Is a joint sitting allowed for an amendment Bill?

No

Can the President refuse assent to an amendment Bill?

No. Assent is compulsory (24th Amendment, 1971)

What is a special majority?

A majority of the total membership + two-thirds of the members present and voting

Is a special majority "two-thirds of the total members"?

No. The two-thirds is of members present and voting

Do all amendments need the approval of States?

No. Only federal provisions need approval of half of the States

Who made the basic structure doctrine?

The Supreme Court, in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

Is the basic structure written in the Constitution?

No. It is a judge-made doctrine

Which amendment is called the "Mini-Constitution"?

The 42nd Amendment (1976)

Which amendment brought the Tenth Schedule?

52nd (1985)

Which amendment brought GST?

101st (2016)

How many amendments are there?

106 (latest: 106th, 2023)

Does creating a new State need Article 368?

No. It needs only a simple majority law under Articles 2 and 3

10. Quick Revision Points

Article 368 (Part XX): power and procedure to amend.

Introduced only in Parliament; no joint sitting; President must assent (24th Amendment).

Three types: simple majority; special majority; special majority + half of the States.

Special majority: majority of total membership + two-thirds of present and voting.

Federal provisions (President's election, Supreme Court, High Courts, Seventh Schedule, Article 368, representation of States) need half of the State Legislatures.

Case order: Shankari Prasad (1951) → Sajjan Singh (1965) → Golak Nath (1967) → 24th Amendment (1971) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) → Minerva Mills (1980) → Waman Rao (1981) → I.R. Coelho (2007).

Kesavananda: 13 judges; 7:6; basic structure.

Minerva Mills: struck down Article 368(4) and (5) added by the 42nd Amendment.

Important amendments: 1st (Ninth Schedule), 7th (States reorganisation), 42nd (Mini-Constitution), 44th (property), 52nd (anti-defection), 61st (voting age 18), 73rd and 74th (local bodies), 86th (education), 91st, 101st (GST), 103rd (EWS), 104th, 105th, 106th (women's reservation).

Total amendments: 106 (as of mid-2026).
